title: 9 Things To Do When You're Feeling Burned-Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/05/05/9-things-to-do-when-youre-feeling-burned-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes teacher burnout as a state that rarely resolves on its own and offers nine concrete actions for reversing it. These include jettisoning extra responsibilities and clubs outside contractual duties, learning to say no to anything that isn't a definite yes, physically tidying the classroom for its cathartic and behavioral benefits, and doubling down on classroom management mastery as a hedge against the chaos that most often causes burnout. He also recommends deliberately enjoying teaching each day, mentally leaving school at school, avoiding gossip and school politics to protect focus, creating a personal daily schedule to increase efficiency, and taking a quiet moment each morning to breathe and visualize a calm, successful day. Linsin closes by insisting burnout requires active intervention rather than passive endurance, framing it as fixable through small, deliberate changes rather than an unavoidable part of the job.
points: Burnout rarely fixes itself and tends to worsen without deliberate action, even though vacations offer temporary relief.
Dropping non-contractual responsibilities and learning to say no are presented as high-leverage fixes for overload.
Mastering classroom management principles is framed as the most durable hedge against the misbehavior-driven stress that fuels burnout.
Mentally "leaving school at school" and avoiding gossip or politics protect a teacher's energy and focus.
A daily practice of quiet breathing and visualization builds a sense of control that directly counters burnout's helpless feeling.
quotes: The problem with this approach is that burnout rarely fixes itself. Sure, a vacation can ease the problem temporarily.
Simply spending less time at work, and having less to concern yourself with, can be just the balm you need to feel fresh and looking forward to each day.
The idea that teachers are somehow expected to leave their health and contentment, and even families, on the altar of education—which its culture sometimes perpetuates—is shameful.

Misbehavior, disrespect, noisiness, chaos, excitability . . . these are the chief reasons teachers become burned-out. A kind, well-behaved classroom, on the other hand, is an impenetrable hedge against ever feeling this way.

And if ever you feel guilty about leaving school at a decent hour, just remind yourself that you’re far more effective when you have a chance to get away, gain perspective, and recharge your batteries.

The good news is that it usually doesn’t take a lot to fix. A simple change in routine, attitude, or approach like any of those noted above can put you on a new and happier course in a matter of days.
